title: Like a trumpeter
hookLine: the four immeasurables sounded in every direction, like a strong trumpeter

cards: Long before loudspeakers, a strong player could lift a conch shell and send one clear note out over the fields. He doesn't aim it. He doesn't send it down one road.
The sound simply goes out, and nobody within reach is left out of hearing it. The Pali word for him is sankhadhama: a conch-blower.

That is the picture the Buddha reaches for near the end of the Tevijja Sutta, the thirteenth of the Long Discourses. Yesterday he took apart a claim. Today he hands the young brahmin Vasettha something to do instead.

teach.h: WHAT IS BRAHMA LIKE? FREE OF HATE.
teach.b: Vasettha and his friend wanted the straight road to union with Brahma, the high god of their teachers. The Buddha has just shown that their teachers never saw Brahma. But he doesn't walk away.
He asks: is Brahma, as you describe him, full of hate or free of it? Free of it, they say. Burdened with possessions or free of them?
Free. Then he describes a monk who becomes like that. First, the monk lets go of the five hindrances, and gladness rises.
Then he lets a mind of loving-kindness fill one direction, then the second, the third, the fourth, then above, below, around, everywhere: a mind wide, grown great, without measure, free of hate.
Then the same with compassion. Then with gladness at others' joy. Then with equanimity.
Elsewhere the texts call these four the brahmaviharas, the dwellings of Brahma; they're also called the four immeasurables. And here's the image.
As a strong trumpeter makes himself heard in all four directions without any strain, so this mind leaves out no living thing. It doesn't choose who gets to hear. Here is the move.
The Buddha takes the brahmins' own goal, union with Brahma, and gives it content. Not a place you travel to by argument, but a heart you grow, one direction at a time.

In a number of Buddhist communities the four are still practiced this way, radiating outward, direction by direction. And the image carries one more detail: the conch-blower is heard with little difficulty.

how: In many Buddhist traditions people practice the four brahmaviharas by sending loving-kindness, compassion, appreciative joy and equanimity outward in each direction in turn, often as part of a daily sit or a chanted metta practice.

o: a heaven reached by reciting the Vedas
a temple built to honor the god Brahma
a dwelling of Brahma: the four immeasurables

games.q: like a trumpeter: tap the pairs.
p: the young brahmin who asked the way
heard in all directions, without strain

s: after showing the brahmins' teachers never saw Brahma, the Buddha simply leaves
he goes on to teach a way to become like Brahma: the four immeasurables.
in DN 13 the mind of loving-kindness is spread one direction after another, then everywhere
first one quarter, then the second, third and fourth, then above, below and all around.
the trumpeter in the image has to strain to be heard
the point is ease: he is heard in all four directions without difficulty.

games.q: you're the Buddha. you've just shown two young brahmins that their teachers never saw the god they describe. they still want union with Brahma. what do you do?
o: tell them to drop the goal entirely.
ask what Brahma is like, then teach a heart that becomes like that.
send them back to their teachers.
games.why: he asks whether Brahma is free of hate, then teaches the four immeasurables as the way to become like Brahma.

practice: Pick one of the four, kindness, compassion, gladness for others or calm, and let it face forward, then to your right, behind you, to your left, then above and below.
You don't need to picture anyone; let the wish go out the way a note goes out, without pushing. If it goes thin, come back to the breath and send it again.

wordCard.voice: Brahmavihara. The four immeasurables from the Tevijja Sutta: a mind of goodwill heard in every direction, leaving no one out, without strain. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali brahmavihara: a dwelling of Brahma. the name for the four immeasurables.

carryVoice: Your line: the note isn't forced. A heart grown wide reaches everyone without strain. Rest well.

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 13 (Tevijja Sutta), the four brahmaviharas and the trumpeter simile
